1.pericope_label: I cried unto God with my voice, even unto God with my voice; and he gave ear unto me

debates.q: Is the grief personal or national?

sides.view: National — a common form of prayer dictated for the Church in affliction
National, since the consolation sought is in the nation’s own history
The captive Israelites speak, though the psalm suits any soul in distress
One man under prevailing melancholy, in whom drooping saints see themselves

debates.q: What does the clause rendered my sore ran in the night mean?

sides.view: My hand was stretched out — a night spent with voice and hands lifted up
The text is faulty and probably beyond recovery; eye may stand where we read hand
The night, which to others was a time of rest, is the point

outliers.view: Turns the opening cry into a rebuke, observing that men cry to the Lord for riches, safety and dignity, but scarce one for the sake of the Lord himself

4.pericope_label: Thou holdest mine eyes waking: I am so troubled that I cannot speak

debates.q: Are his eyes held open or held shut?

sides.view: Shut — God has closed the guards of his eyes, and the received version reverses the voice
Open — God keeps the watches of his eyes and grief forbids sleep

debates.q: Do the questions of these verses speak unbelief or faith?

sides.view: The versions differ: the Syriac makes them affirmations of unbelief, the Arabic mere inquiry, the Targum an appeal of faith
They are pleading and reasoning with God about the length of the captivity
The casting off feared is of the peculiar people, not the poet alone

outliers.view: Answers the rhetorical question about shut-up mercies in the affirmative, holding that the spring was diverted from the Jews to the Gentiles
Doubts the psalmist had a harp at all in the captivity, while supposing the following three verses to be the ode he sang on it

10.pericope_label: And I said, This is my infirmity: but I will remember the years of the right hand of the most High

debates.q: What does the tenth verse say?

sides.view: To grieve is my portion; to change my condition belongs to the Most High
Such despair is on my part profanation — a kind of blasphemy against past grace
Either self-correction for questioning God’s love, or comfort that the sickness is not to death
The long affliction was allotted by the Sovereign Lord; the rest is supplied by translators
In the sanctuary, where doubts are solved and fears dissipated
With the holy — that is, with Israel
In holiness: God is just and true in all his works

outliers.view: Makes despair itself a profanation, so that doubting continued help from a God gracious in the past counts as blasphemy
Notes that the same remedy failed the psalmist earlier in the psalm and worked on the second attempt, and draws from it a rule about persevering in means

16.pericope_label: The waters saw thee, O God, the waters saw thee; they were afraid

debates.q: What is the vault of the eighteenth verse?

sides.view: The vault of heaven, from a root meaning to roll; the modern preference for whirlwind is strange
The orb, that is the air, so called because spherical
The whirlwind, the storm driven on like a chariot

debates.q: Why are the footsteps not known?

sides.view: Because God is without parts or limits and no object of sense
Because the water returned and covered them
Because the obscuring was itself part of the lesson

outliers.view: Admits the storm at the Red Sea is absent from the narrative of Moses, and corroborates it from Josephus rather than from Scripture
Defends the abrupt ending of the psalm as the best close available, against those who take it for unfinished
